title: Understand multiplication as equal groups, arrays, skip-counting and repeated addition

lesson.title: What Multiplication Really Means: Equal Groups

steps.say: You already know how to skip-count really well, like counting by twenty-fives and hundreds. Today we use that same skip-counting idea to find out how many things are in a bunch of equal groups, without counting one by one.

Imagine you are making muffins for a class party. You put three muffins on each plate, and you have four plates. Every plate has the same amount, so these are equal groups. You could add three plus three plus three plus three, and that gives twelve. Multiplication is just a shortcut for that: four groups of three is four times three, and it equals twelve.

Now let us line those muffins up in neat rows instead. Four rows, with three in each row. This tidy rectangle is called an array. Skip-count down the rows with me: three, six, nine, twelve. Same twelve muffins, same four times three. Equal groups and arrays are two pictures of the very same idea.
Here is the skip-counting on a number line. Start at zero and jump three, four times. Three, six, nine, twelve. Each jump is one group, and where you land is your answer.

Now here is a mistake lots of kids make. Someone sees three times four and writes seven. But seven is what you get when you add three and four. Times does not mean add the two numbers. Three times four means three groups with four in each group. Count them: four, eight, twelve. So three times four is twelve, not seven. Whenever you see the times sign, whisper to yourself, groups of.
So remember, the times sign is really saying groups of, and you can always check it by skip-counting.

lesson.answer: The times sign means ‘groups of’ — four times three is four groups of three, which is twelve.

practice.question: At the Vancouver farmers market, granola bars come in small boxes. Each box holds four granola bars, and you buy six boxes. Draw six groups with four dots in each group, then skip-count by fours to find how many granola bars you have altogether. Write it as a multiplication sentence too.
practice.answer: Skip-counting by fours: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24. Six times four equals twenty-four, so you have 24 granola bars.
